questions.q: What is the most common real-world cause of an accidental Cartesian product?
options: A missing or incomplete ON condition on what was meant to be a normal join
Explicitly typing CROSS JOIN by mistake
Using WHERE instead of HAVING
Forgetting to add an ORDER BY clause
questions.explain: Old-style comma joins with no ON at all, or a JOIN with a missing/wrong ON clause, are the classic real-world triggers.

questions.q: Why is 'ON p.Name IS NOT NULL' a dangerous ON clause?
options: It evaluates to TRUE for nearly every row combination, producing a Cartesian product in disguise, while looking syntactically correct
It causes a syntax error
It only matches rows where Name is genuinely NULL
It has no effect on the join at all
questions.explain: This is subtler than a missing ON clause entirely, because the query looks structurally correct at a glance.

questions.q: If Production.Product has ~500 rows and Sales.SalesOrderDetail has 100,000, how many rows does an accidental Cartesian product between them produce?
options: About 50 million (500 × 100,000)
Exactly 100,000
Exactly 500
questions.explain: Row counts multiply, not add — this is the same principle from Lesson 26, applied to a real accidental scenario.

questions.q: What practical habit helps catch an accidental Cartesian product before it reaches production?
options: Sanity-check the resulting row count after writing any join — millions of rows from small tables is a red flag
Always add TOP 1000000 to every query
Never use INNER JOIN, only CROSS JOIN
Only use subqueries, never joins
questions.explain: A join between small-to-medium tables returning millions of rows should immediately prompt re-checking the ON clause.

questions.q: What does an old-style comma join (FROM TableA, TableB) with no WHERE or ON condition produce?
options: A Cartesian product, since SQL Server has no basis for matching rows
A syntax error
An empty result set
The same result as an INNER JOIN automatically
questions.explain: Without any join condition, SQL Server pairs every row of one table with every row of the other.
